stories.headline: Update: Russian Strikes Kill at Least 15 in Kyiv Region; Boy, 7, Pulled Alive From Rubble
stories.summary:
Overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the Kyiv region, killed nine people when a residential building was hit at about 05:00 local time Sunday, while families were asleep. A seven-year-old boy was pulled alive from the rubble after about 14 hours and is in stable condition in hospital. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive. Regional head Tymur Tkachenko said others were still missing.

A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze. President Volodymyr Zelensky said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike that hit a grocery store in Vyshneve. Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, according to Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky.

Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said more than 70 strikes had been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening. Zelensky said more than 130 emergency workers were at the Dymer site, and that rescue efforts were complicated by constant new air raid alerts. Russia's defense ministry said its forces struck targets including a power station, port infrastructure and a cargo ship.

The attacks continue a heavy Russian bombardment of Ukraine and come as Zelensky has publicly criticized Trump's description of Putin as a friend, while Ukraine defends its own strikes on the Crimean Bridge as a fair response.

stories.headline: Update: Clayton Says Americans Should Expect 'Bumps in the Road' as Infrastructure Is Upgraded Amid Outages
stories.summary:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Sunday that Americans should prepare for a great deal of investment in the country's aging infrastructure and systems, and warned of "bumps in the road." Appearing on CNN's State of the Union, he said the public should expect "glitches, gaps, and interruptions in service" as technology systems upgrade in the era of artificial intelligence.

His remarks follow a series of outages affecting businesses and air travel. On Sunday, an issue with Delta Air Lines' weight and balance automation system delayed hundreds of flights, centered on its Atlanta hub, and the FAA issued an hourlong ground stop for some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson. The FAA said the delays were not related to air traffic control. Delta said it resolved the outage, though weather created further delays in the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The comments come after the White House ousted the national cyber director and President Trump said a week of tech outages was unrelated. Bloomberg reported that the White House is responding to aviation infrastructure problems as affordability and domestic concerns take on greater political importance.

Clayton's message frames the disruptions as the cost of modernization rather than a sign of coordinated failure, though critics are likely to press the administration on preparedness as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January.

stories.headline: Update: Democrats Win Largest House Majority Since 1992 After Flipping North Carolina Seat
stories.summary:
Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina's 5th District, a race called Sunday after a recount. Hubbard led by 330 votes with 99 percent counted. Foxx, who has represented the district since 2005, had requested the recount, which state law allows when the margin is under 1 percent, and she conceded Sunday.

The result brings Democrats to at least 258 House seats against at least 173 for Republicans, with four races still uncalled. That ties the party's 258-seat total from 1992, the last time either party won as many House races. Democrats also secured the Senate in the midterms. Remaining contests include Tennessee's 4th District, where Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and Minnesota's 1st, where Democrat Jake Johnson leads by fewer than 500. Two Louisiana races go to a December runoff.

Hubbard campaigned on the rising cost of living during the war with Iran, which was a top issue for voters. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have suggested that war-related inflation was probably to blame for Republican losses. Foxx said she ran on a record of commonsense solutions and conservative values and came up a few votes short.

Democrats could use their majorities to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, and the Senate can confirm or block cabinet and judicial nominations. They can also pass legislation more easily, though Trump retains final sign-off, and Republicans have only a few weeks left to advance priorities before the new Congress takes over.

stories.headline: Sen.-Elect El-Sayed Says He Would Pass Medicare for All as 'TrumpCare'
stories.summary:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat, said Sunday on NBC's Meet the Press that he would pass a single-payer health bill, commonly called Medicare for All, under the name TrumpCare. He said he does not really care what it is called. Host Kristen Welker had raised President Donald Trump's potential role in the question.

Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, a Minnesota Democrat, joined him in courting Trump's backing. She said people are ready for Medicare for All and that calling it TrumpCare is fine if that gets it across the finish line.

The overture comes as Democrats prepare to control both chambers in January, and Trump has signaled openness to working with the incoming Democratic Congress in some areas. Supporters of single-payer see the branding offer as a pragmatic way to win presidential support. Conservative critics and many Republicans have long opposed such a system over its cost and the expanded federal role in health care, and Trump has not endorsed the idea.

stories.headline: NRC Approves Construction of Four Advanced Reactors at Dow Plant in Texas
stories.summary:
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has issued a construction permit for four Xe-100 small modular reactors at Dow's Seadrift chemical site in Texas. It is the first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in the United States in more than half a century.

Supporters, including a National Review analysis, credit President Trump's cutting of nuclear regulatory red tape last year for the approval and call it a sign of a nuclear renaissance. The plant would supply industrial energy to the chemical facility.

The approval is a milestone for advanced reactor developers, though construction, costs and eventual operation remain ahead. Critics of rapid deregulation have raised safety and oversight concerns, while proponents say streamlined review is needed to meet rising electricity demand.

stories.headline: Update: Army Plans Iowa Lead Azide Detonation by Nov. 24 Despite Court Pause
stories.summary:
The US Army said in a court filing Saturday that it intends to proceed with detonating about five tonnes of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, despite a court order pausing the plan indefinitely. The Justice Department told the court that "protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay." The Army now plans to act by Nov. 24 under an emergency exemption.

The Army argues that falling temperatures, expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit in the coming days, raise the risk of an unplanned explosion. It said it removed the doors of the bunker holding the barrels in preparation for the detonation, leaving the material more vulnerable to temperature changes. The Environmental Protection Agency granted an emergency permit covering 68 drums, citing an imminent and substantial threat.

The Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club sued Thursday, arguing the Army failed to consider safer alternatives, and the court ordered the pause. The groups said many Iowans in the risk zone were unaware of the plan. "There is no safe level of lead exposure," the council said. The groups filed a new motion Sunday. The Army has not released details of the rescheduled detonation, though it earlier advised residents to leave homes for about six hours.

The new development is the Army's filing signaling it will move ahead notwithstanding the court's pause.

stories.headline: Director of National Intelligence Says Putin Is 'Not America's Friend in Ukraine'
stories.summary:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton defended President Trump's use of the word "friend" for Russian President Vladimir Putin while drawing a distinction between the leaders' personal relationship and that of the two countries. Clayton made the remarks in an interview Sunday on ABC's "This Week" with co-anchor Jonathan Karl.

Clayton said Putin is not America's friend in Ukraine, separating Mr. Trump's personal rapport with the Russian leader from the interests of the United States. The comments follow Mr. Trump's description of Putin as a friend, which drew a sharp response from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who called Putin a killer while Russian strikes on Ukraine continued.

Supporters of the president generally say personal engagement with adversaries is a tool of diplomacy and can help secure negotiated outcomes. Critics, including many Democrats and some Republicans, argue that warm language toward Putin undercuts Ukraine and sends mixed signals while Russian attacks kill civilians. Clayton's remarks represent an administration effort to clarify the distinction.

The interview is among several Sunday show appearances in which administration officials addressed the president's security agenda.

stories.headline: US Power Advantage Over China Shrinks to Smallest Level Since 2018, Report Finds
stories.summary:
The advantage the United States holds over China in influencing international events has shrunk to its smallest level since 2018, according to a new report cited by Bloomberg. The report attributes the decline to the war with Iran and to unilateralism, which it says are undermining American military and diplomatic strength.

The findings come as President Trump told an Israeli outlet that he may not decide on his next move in the Iran war until 2027. Tensions remain high, and an Iranian missile and drone attack recently started a fire at an industrial facility in Bahrain.

On China, the United States is divided between the concerns of the national security establishment and the prospect of expanded trade. Supporters of the administration argue that its assertive approach restores deterrence and leverage, while critics say unilateral actions have alienated allies and strained resources. The report's measures of influence are one assessment among many and are contested.

stories.headline: Update: Trump and Democrats Probe Areas of Cooperation as Van Hollen Presses Senate Leadership Bid
stories.summary:
On Sunday's political talk shows, incoming Democratic leaders and the White House outlined possible areas of cooperation and conflict ahead of Democrats taking control of Congress in January. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who was nominated for speaker, told CBS's Face the Nation about areas where Democrats could explore coming together with President Trump, who said Friday he is open to great healthcare. Bloomberg reporting pointed to credit card interest rates, healthcare and immigration as possible areas of overlap.

In the Senate, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland pressed his challenge to Minority Leader Chuck Schumer on Meet the Press, saying momentum is in his direction and that the party needs new leadership to deliver on the economic promises that helped it win the midterms. He has also described himself as the underdog. Trump said it would be very hard to work with Schumer as majority leader and predicted he would fail again.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota have courted Trump on universal healthcare, suggesting it could be called Trumpcare. Trump responded publicly on Saturday. Conservative commentators, including Washington Examiner's Byron York, argued Democrats may declare victory on affordability and turn to oversight, while some Democrats, such as Bill de Blasio, urged colleagues to focus on cost of living rather than partisan probes.

Tension remains over oversight and war policy. Trump has issued an order requiring federal contractors to notify the White House of congressional requests, which Republicans defend as protecting privileged communications and Democrats view as obstruction. House Democrats are also divided over whether to demand an end to Iran war funding now, risking a shutdown, or wait until they control Congress.

stories.headline: Delta Outage Delays Thousands of Flights Nationwide, Centered on Atlanta Hub
stories.summary:
A failure in Delta Air Lines' weight-and-balance automation system caused widespread flight delays on Sunday, hitting Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the world's busiest, and the airline's network nationwide. The Federal Aviation Administration said on X that Delta was working to resolve the problem and that the delays were not related to FAA air traffic control systems.

The system calculates the weight and balance of departing aircraft, a required step before takeoff. Delta said crews were using manual workarounds, and reports put the number of delayed flights at no fewer than 3,500. The FAA said all Delta flights through Atlanta were affected, and disruptions spread to other hubs, including major California airports.

The timing, days before Thanksgiving, raised the stakes for holiday travelers. The disruption follows a nationwide ground stop that canceled thousands of flights last weekend and a roughly 10-day wave of tech outages across American institutions.

Lawmakers have warned that power grids, water systems and banks are soft targets, and the White House has fired its national cyber director amid the outages. Officials have not tied the Delta problem to the earlier incidents, and the airline has not given a cause or a timeline for full recovery.

stories.headline: Update: Zelensky Defends Crimean Bridge Strikes as 'Fair Response' as UK Defence Secretary Visits Kyiv
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the BBC in Kyiv that Ukraine's repeated attacks on the bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea were a fair response to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine. This week's combined missile and drone strikes destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it and one of its two support arches into the sea and making it unusable for road traffic.

Zelensky rejected Vladimir Putin's claim that the bridge is exclusively civilian, pointing to images of Russian tanks and military hardware using the route as a supply line. He said the intense Russian attacks that followed were a signal that Putin does not want to stop and wants a pretext to escalate.

Russian strikes continued overnight. A seven-year-old boy was killed on a playground in Kryvyi Rih, Zelensky's hometown, along with a 20-year-old female medic, and 58 people were injured. Local officials said the site was struck again with jet-powered drones as rescuers arrived.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting met Zelensky, saying he was there to show Europe was united. He called Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday during Coalition of the Willing exercises an outrageous provocation and said the timing seemed more than a coincidence. He said the best response was to do more for Ukraine and called Putin a cold-blooded killer.

stories.headline: Update: 11 Killed in Violence in Sinaloa After Capture of Cartel Leader 'El Chapo Isidro'
stories.summary:
At least 11 people were killed in a burst of violence in Mexico's Sinaloa state following the capture of cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," authorities said Saturday. The arrest of the man, who was among the FBI's 10 most-wanted fugitives, set off a fierce gun battle on Friday that turned an elite military operation into a night of chaos. Helicopters fired from above and explosions rocked the ground as armed militants mounted a counterattack against security forces.

Meza Flores climbed the cartel ranks to lead part of the Beltran Leyva organization and later headed his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. He is accused of drug trafficking and torture, and of smuggling narcotics into the United States for more than two decades. A U.S. official described him as the most dangerous man in Mexico.

U.S. and Mexican authorities shared intelligence for weeks to track him. The operation was aimed at dismantling his influence and could reshape the power struggle within the Sinaloa Cartel's territory. The earlier capture was previously reported; the new development is the death toll from the ensuing violence, which authorities say continued after the arrest.

stories.headline: Appeals Court Rules $1.7 Trillion 2022 Spending Bill Unconstitutional Over Proxy Voting
stories.summary:
The New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 9-8 on Friday that the $1.7 trillion government funding bill passed in 2022 under then-President Joe Biden was unconstitutional. The court found that the pandemic-era House rule allowing lawmakers to vote by proxy violated the Constitution's Quorum Clause, which governs the presence of members needed to conduct business.

The narrow en banc decision centers on whether the bill was validly passed when proxy votes counted toward the quorum. Critics of proxy voting, who have largely been conservatives, argue the Constitution requires lawmakers to be physically present. Supporters of the rule have said it was a reasonable accommodation during the pandemic and that chambers hold broad authority over their own procedures.

The practical consequences of the ruling and the likelihood of further appeal were not immediately detailed. The case could be headed to the Supreme Court, where the justices would weigh the limits of congressional rulemaking power and the status of legislation passed under the contested procedure.

stories.headline: Republicans Debate Causes of Midterm Losses and Trump's Role Ahead of 2028
stories.summary:
A divide is emerging inside the Republican Party over what caused its wipeout midterm defeats, according to reporting from The New York Times and Politico. Some grassroots GOP leaders want President Trump to stay out of the 2028 race, even as they acknowledge he is unlikely to do so. The debate foreshadows a battle over the party's direction.

Conservative commentary has focused heavily on prices. National Review's Charles C. W. Cooke wrote that gas prices and the general cost of living were the obvious explanation, noting that Democratic billboards across the South highlighted rising costs without mentioning party affiliation. He also pointed to Trump's tariff agenda and a war launched without explanation as sources of voter discontent.

Other Republicans argue the losses reflect broader factors, while Trump allies have resisted blaming the president. Democrats say the results were a rebuke of administration policies and will take control of the House in January, with Hakeem Jeffries nominated for Speaker. The intraparty fight is expected to intensify as 2028 positioning begins.

stories.headline: Sunday Shows to Focus on Trump's Security Agenda and House Leadership
stories.summary:
The Sunday political talk shows are expected to center on President Trump's national security agenda and the leadership transition in the House. House Democrats nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker this week, which would make him the first Black lawmaker to lead the chamber. Rep. Katherine Clark was elected as the first woman in her leadership post.

The discussion comes as Trump issued an executive order late Friday directing federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House of congressional requests for their communications and to withhold material the administration deems privileged. The order is widely seen as an effort to blunt expected aggressive oversight from Democrats when they take control of Congress in January. Companies that fail to comply could risk losing contracts.

The administration says it is protecting executive privilege, while Democrats and critics describe the move as an attempt to stymie legitimate oversight. Expect lawmakers from both parties to be pressed on the order and on the coming investigations.

stories.headline: Update: Jeffries Nominated for Speaker as Trump Signals Openness to Compromise With Incoming Democratic Congress
stories.summary:
House Democrats this week nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for the Speakership, setting up what would be his historic election as the first Black lawmaker to lead the chamber. Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) was also elected to a leadership post as the first woman in her role. Democrats took the House and the Senate in the midterms, and several House races remain uncalled. The 119th Congress left town Saturday after a week of confirmations and bills, with Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and other leaders voicing frustration over low attendance.

President Trump said Saturday in a Fox News interview with Kayleigh McEnany that the Democratic-controlled Congress presents an opportunity to compromise on immigration and health care. He offered rare praise for Jeffries even after Jeffries called top aide Stephen Miller a "stone-cold racist"; Trump defended Miller as a "good person." Jeffries told The New York Times he is open to working with Republicans but has not yet spoken extensively with GOP leaders.

The administration is also bracing for oversight. Late Friday Trump signed an executive order directing federal contractors to notify the White House of congressional requests for their communications and to withhold material the administration deems privileged. Republicans and administration allies describe it as protecting executive confidentiality, while Democrats and critics say it is an attempt to stymie oversight before they take control in January. Democrats are also expected to scrutinize ICE tactics, after masked agents detained two people on a Seattle-Tacoma airport jet bridge Saturday, prompting condemnation from Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson.

Republicans, meanwhile, are debating the causes of the midterm losses. Some, such as former Sen. Sam Brownback, say voters rejected Trump personally rather than his policies, citing inflation and gas prices, while others are already positioning for the 2028 nomination.

stories.headline: Update: Zelensky Calls Putin a 'Killer' After Trump Calls Him a Friend; Russian Strikes Continue
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN that Vladimir Putin is a "killer" and an enemy, responding to Donald Trump calling the Russian leader his "friend" before Thursday's trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Zelensky said it was up to Trump how to describe Putin, but that such language suggests Putin "doesn't feel enough pressure." Trump, speaking Friday, doubled down on the description, said Putin would "love to end the war," and said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

Russian attacks continued overnight. Officials said two people were killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih, with more injuries in Kharkiv and Rivne. On Friday at least nine people were killed in strikes on Kyiv bridges and western railway stations, in what Zelensky called the biggest attack this year: 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

Zelensky told the BBC that Ukraine's strikes on the Crimean Bridge were a "fair response" to 109 Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges, rejecting Putin's claim that the span is purely civilian. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting visited Kyiv to show European unity and called a Russian cruise missile that hit Poland during coalition exercises an "outrageous provocation." Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said the missiles' guidance systems make it very unlikely they strayed off course because of Ukrainian electronic warfare. Poland has called the incident a provocation, and no injuries were reported.

stories.headline: Update: COP31 Climate Talks Go Into Overtime With Fossil Fuels Absent From Draft Deal
stories.summary:
The United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, extended into an unscheduled extra day on Saturday as negotiators sought a final agreement, even as work crews boxed up the venue. Hopes are slim that the added talks will yield concrete plans to cut fossil fuel use. The draft final text has drawn strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels.

A letter sent Saturday by 100 civil society groups to the co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, warned they were on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UN has held, with only hours left to save it. Observers at the venue described a bleak atmosphere with dwindling food and water and no sign of progress. Teresa Anderson of ActionAid International said no one knows what is happening behind closed doors.

The backdrop is stark. The UN said before the talks that the world will likely overshoot the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, and Climate Action Tracker found progress has stalled for five years. Experts say drastic cuts to coal, oil and gas emissions are needed to avert the worst effects, while vulnerable nations, including small island states, are pressing for stronger action. The outcome of the extended session is the main development to watch.

stories.headline: South Korea's Education Minister Resigns Over College Exam Cheating Scandal
stories.summary:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned Sunday over the cheating scandal and chaotic countermeasures surrounding Thursday's national college entrance exam, the Suneung. President Lee Jae Myung, who has called for an overhaul of the exam system, accepted the resignation. Choi said he could not escape criticism that the government failed to prepare in advance.

The crisis began a week earlier when Han Won-seok, the top scorer on April's national tax accountancy exam, admitted using a micro-camera, a phone and AI tools to cheat. In response, authorities rushed in new measures just days before the Suneung, which about 500,000 students took. For the first time, the national disaster alert system was used to catch cheaters, with three alerts sounding on phones nationwide between 08:00 and 15:00, even on silent mode and on tourists' roaming phones.

Candidates also had to cover buttons on clothing and submit to eyewear inspections, which left even honest test takers anxious. The education ministry said 111 candidates were found with unauthorized smart devices. The exam heavily shapes career paths for millions of South Koreans, and the episode has intensified debate over academic dishonesty in the age of AI.
